title: Why does the -O4 compiler directive give unexpected results?
body_html:
I'm supposed to use the compiler directives gcc -pedantic -Wall -ansi -O4. But the -O4 flag is giving me some problems. It works without the O4 flag but with it I get unexpected results:

$ gcc -pedantic -Wall -ansi openshell.c 
$ ./a.out 
'PATH' is set to /home/dac/proj/google-cloud-sdk/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games.
miniShell>> ls | wc -l
82
6318: child 6319 status 0x0000
Execution time 1.197 ms
miniShell>> exit
$ gcc -pedantic -Wall -ansi -O4 openshell.c 
$ ./a.out 
'PATH' is set to /home/dac/proj/google-cloud-sdk/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games.
miniShell>> ls | wc -l
./a.out:6332: Syntax error: pipe with no command following (10: No child processes)

What can I do about it? The relevant code is:

static void exec_arguments(int argc, char **argv)
{
    /* Split the command line into sequences of arguments */
    /* Break at pipe symbols as arguments on their own */

    int i = 1;

    char ***cmdv = malloc(sizeof *cmdv * (argc/2));       
    char **args = malloc(sizeof *args * (argc+1));
    int cmdn = 0;
    int argn = 0;

    cmdv[cmdn++] = &args[argn];

    for (i=1; i < argc; i++)
    {
        char *arg = argv[i];
        if (strcmp(arg, "|") == 0)
        {
            if (i == 1)
                err_sysexit("Syntax error: pipe before any command");
            if (args[argn-1] == 0)
                err_sysexit("Syntax error: two pipes with no command between");
            arg = 0;
        }
        args[argn++] = arg;
        if (arg == 0)
            cmdv[cmdn++] = &args[argn];
    }
    if (args[argn-1] == 0)
        err_sysexit("Syntax error: pipe with no command following");
    args[argn] = 0;

    exec_pipeline(cmdn, cmdv);
    free(cmdv);
    free(args);
}

It happens if I compile with O3 and O4 but not with O2. The call to the above function is this code:

 argv2[1] = line;
 i = 1;
 p = strtok (line, " ");


 while (p != NULL)
 {
   array[i++] = p;
   p = strtok (NULL, " ");
 }
 exec_arguments(i, array);
 corpse_collector();

events.body_html: There's a -O4 flag? Options That Control Optimization
Is -O4 actually supported by GCC? ISTR running into problems with it, and -O3 was actually the maximum...but I'd expect a compiler warning rather than errors.
@JonathanLeffler It happens if I compile using -O3 as well but not using -O2.

Most likely, there's some undefined behaviour in your code, and using optimization is revealing it. Have you printed out your inputs and your outputs? Three-star programming is worrying — not automatically wrong, but harder to get right. Have you ensured you have null-terminated your argument lists? It's going to be hard for anyone to help much without some information about what's in the argc and argv you pass to the function (example values). Ideally, you'd provide an MCVE (minimal reproducible example).
Try running your code through valgrind or similar; there may be some allocation issues.
@JonathanLeffler I added the code which makes the call to the function. I'm going to try and reproduce it as an MCVE.
Thanks for the extra info. Why do you start at 1 rather than 0 with the indexes? Why are you using argv[2] for the initial assignment and array[i++] thereafter?

@JonathanLeffler I will provide more context. I put the code here. I read in a command line including a pipeline e.g. ls | wc -l and then I split it and execute the command. The project is my own small shell and I'm working on pipelining. Pipelining is working except for this optimization level. I also included the valgrind output in the question now.

@JonathanLeffler I start at 1 rather than 0 because 0 would be the name of the program (?) and the args should be the commands in the pipeline. The argv[2] might be clutter, I'm checking what is it and I think it is some leftover from a rewrite. It would be interesting if we can find what is the matter with the code.

I have a negative result — I can't reproduce the problem on my Mac with my dummy exec_pipeline() and main() based on your calling fragment. I'll download the code (16 KiB — thanks for not posting all that up front) and I'll see if I can make head or tail of it.

And now I have a positive result — with your code I can repro the problem.  I'm also suffering from some deja vu — I think I recognize some of the code.  Not got a definitive read on what's going wrong yet, though.

@JonathanLeffler I wrote a shell and now I want to implement pipelining so I'm using some code from an SO answer that you gave how to implement pipelining. You had a program named pipeline.c and I'm using the functions.
Let us continue this discussion in chat.

Regarding -O4, gcc accepts any number after -O (or at least anything up to 99 works for sure - I don't really know about larger numbers) and will set the optimization level to the highest supported. Some projects use -O99; I guess they figure that if gcc ups the optimization ante, then they're ready to go with it.
Note: Being a 3-star C programmer is not a compliment. And the multiple indirection looks fishy.

Thank you. I put in a debug statement that logs to dev/null and then the loop doesn't crash (but we don't know why). I'm going to review the code, but for now my problem is solved when I put in a dummy debug statement. Maybe I can make an example that works with clang and not with gcc and with fixed input and compare the assembly and see what is the matter really.

There is a bug in your program. The -O4 option doesn't do anything different from -O3. A quick look at man gcc would've enumerated the list of options that do anything, and a sanity check:

diff <(gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O4) <(gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O3)

shows no difference.

Typically changing optimization levels is a good way to find bugs in your program as it may behave perfectly fine in one optimization level or break in another. This is indicative of undefined behavior, etc. I'm not going to waste my time debugging your program for you but at least you know that the problem is not directly caused by -O4.

Sidenote: I'm assuming that -ansi is a requirement that you can't change, however that compiles in C90 mode, aka ancient C mode. I would recommend C99 or C11 to avoid surprises.

After taking a pruning hook to the code, I've discovered the cause of trouble.

As I first suggested, the trouble is "most likely, there's some undefined behaviour in your code, and using optimization is revealing it".

The problem is the array in main() defined as char *array[4];. The code overflows that array, leading to undefined behaviour. Changing the size to 40 means the program works reliably.

Although I hacked out large quantities of the code, there are still well over 400 lines of code in the file. I'm sure a more thorough reduction job could be done, but I'm confident that this is the primary cause of the trouble.

Here's the simplified main() function with the too-small setting of char *array[4]l, and two new auxilliary functions, dump_argv() and AllWhiteSpace(). A number of other functions have been removed. The foreground/background stuff has gone; the built-in commands (like cd and exit and unixinfo was removed. The corpse_collector() already collected corpses; the Janitor() function was also trying to collect them, and seldom (okay, I mean never!) found anything because the corpse collector had already done the dirty work. I removed the signal handling as not immediately relevant.

#include <ctype.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

static void dump_argv(const char *tag, int argc, char **argv)
{
    assert(argv != 0 && tag != 0);
    printf("%s: (%d)", tag, argc);
    for (int i = 0; i < argc; i++)
        printf(" {%s}", (argv[i] == NULL) ? "(null)" : argv[i]);
    putchar('\n');
    fflush(stdout);
    assert(argv[argc] == 0);
}

static bool AllWhiteSpace(char *source)
{
    unsigned char c;
    while (isspace(c = *source))
        source++;
    return(c == '\0');
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    err_setarg0(argv[argc-argc]);

    while (1)
    {
        char *p;
        char *array[40];
        char line[BUFFER_LEN];
        size_t length;
        long time;
        struct timeval time_start;
        struct timeval time_end;

        printf("miniShell>> ");
        fflush(stdout);
        if (!fgets(line, BUFFER_LEN, stdin))
        {
            putchar('\n');
            break;
        }

        if (AllWhiteSpace(line))
            continue;

        length = strlen(line);
        if (line[length - 1] == '\n')
            line[length - 1] = '\0';

        gettimeofday(&time_start, NULL);

        printf("Command line: %s\n", line);
        int i = 1;
        p = strtok(line, " ");

        array[0] = NULL;
        while (p != NULL)
        {
            array[i++] = p;
            p = strtok(NULL, " ");
        }
        array[i] = NULL;
        dump_argv("Before exec_arguments", i, array);
        exec_arguments(i, array);
        corpse_collector();

        gettimeofday(&time_end, NULL);
        time = (time_end.tv_sec  - time_start.tv_sec) * 1000000 +
                time_end.tv_usec - time_start.tv_usec;
        printf("Execution time %ld.%03ld ms\n", time / 1000, time % 1000);
    }

    return(0);
}

The symptoms of trouble now are somewhat different — the strings to be executed are not meaningful, and therefore things fail to execute, but increase the space large enough (40 is overkill for the command line in use; 6 is sufficient) and it works fine.
exec_arguments overflows cmdv in many cases. You should increase the size, and/or also test if ( cmdn >= argc/2 ) err_sysexit before each write to cmdv -- including the one before the loop
because the highest supported optimization in gcc is -O3 so anything higher than 3 will result just like 3
